source.title: Valence-Arousal Subspace in LLMs: Circular Emotion Geometry and Multi-Behavioral Control
source.authors: Lihao Sun; Le-Wen Yan; Xiao-Ya Lu; Andrew H. Lee; Jie Zhang; Jing Shao

page_placements.theme: Off-target steering induces refusal (refusal as a fallback state)

record.tranche_reason: The study tests how steering different directions affects refusal and reports that the emotion-derived VA subspace and a near-orthogonal task-specific refusal direction provide distinct routes for refusal control. This refines the single-direction account, although it does not directly reproduce the original all-layer ablation.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reported refusal outcomes from VA steering and the study's own application of the cited task-specific refusal direction. The affective-generation and sycophancy results do not measure a claim version about refusal. Values used only to select or describe methods, and results cited from other work, are not included.
record.test_reason: Primarily a valence–arousal (VA) emotion-geometry paper. It reports refusal rates for two interventions on Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct. Steering along the Arditi et al. contrastive direction bears on V1. A VA arousal axis nearly orthogonal to that direction (86.5°) also moves refusal both ways, against random-direction controls; this bears on V4. The authors read this as 'multiple possible pathways' for refusal. Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B arousal sweeps add V4 evidence. The original all-layer projection ablation is not reproduced.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors' central claims are three. A 2D VA subspace organizes emotion vectors in a circumplex. Its arousal axis gives bidirectional control of refusal and sycophancy across Llama and Qwen3. This works through lexical mediation: refusal and compliance tokens sit in different VA regions. They present the near-orthogonal Arditi direction as stronger but single-task. They call the two complementary, indicating 'multiple possible pathways', and do not claim the VA route replaces the single direction.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives VA axes from emotion-label mean-difference vectors and steers along those axes; it also steers along a cited task-specific refusal direction. It does not perform the original all-layer, all-position projection ablation. The cited direction's extraction and intervention details are not restated here.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary with steering strength, model, and benchmark. Qwen models require larger strengths than Llama; high strengths can increase OOD generation, especially for Qwen3-8B at α = +3.00. The study reports less consistent refusal effects for valence than for arousal.

fits_no_version.finding: Clamping the logits of 21 refusal/compliance signature tokens drops baseline refusal from 86.5% to 26.0%; random-token clamping has no effect. Under VA steering at α=−0.10, clamping cuts refusal from 90.0% to 44.0%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal and its steerability depend on autoregressive reinforcement through a small set of signature tokens (lexical mediation).

fits_no_version.finding: Individual emotion vectors (anger, disgust, sadness, etc.) raise HarmBench refusal to 93–98.5% at |α|=0.1–0.3, matching or exceeding VA arousal (Table 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Many non-refusal contrastive directions can modulate refusal rates when added at all layers.

fits_no_version.finding: The Arditi direction transferred to sycophancy gives U-shaped effects: both signs lower Political Typology sycophancy (77.6%→57.0% and 66.4%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The refusal direction is behavior-specific and does not give monotonic control of other behaviors.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating the top-500 refusal-token-aligned MLP neurons reduces refusal by about 5%, versus ±0.5% for random ablation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron-level refusal-token pathways contribute only weakly to refusal.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the refusal-rate changes. The original all-layer ablation is not reproduced. Qwen results are reported for independently fitted axes and require much larger steering strengths than Llama; some effects at lower strengths are small. The cited contrastive direction is not re-extracted in this study.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Sycophancy, affective-output steering, token-level analyses, and capability evaluations were left out because they do not measure a refusal-claim version in the required way.

untested.parts: Directional ablation at all layers and positions, weight-level removal, and capability preservation under the Arditi direction are not tested. Only signed addition on Llama 3.1-8B is reported.
There is no explicit comparison of affine, cone, or dominant-plus-others models. No test shows whether ablating the Arditi direction leaves VA-driven refusal control intact, or the reverse.
Not tested. VA axes are refit per model, and the Arditi direction is used only in Llama.
Not tested. Qwen3 thinking mode is not discussed.

missing.what: Llama HarmBench refusal under arousal steering at intermediate strengths (α=−0.30: 93.5%; −0.10: 90.0%; +0.10: 82.5%; +0.30: 59.5%). These are less OOD-confounded than the ±0.45 values.
Capability preservation under arousal steering: MATH-500 and IFEval within about 1–2.5 points at |α|≤0.20.
OOD rates by steering strength for Llama (<2% at |α|≤0.20; arousal 29–71% and −valence 84–94% at 0.45).
In-plane component of the Arditi direction has negative VA coordinates (V=−0.058, A=−0.021), so the two directions are not fully disjoint.
Llama HarmBench refusal under arousal steering at α=+0.30 (59%) compared with the Arditi direction at −0.30 (2.0%).

record.verdict_notes: V4 evidence is indirect. The study shows a second near-orthogonal steering direction that changes refusal. It does not show that refusal itself needs a multi-dimensional description. VA effects may act through output-token logits rather than a refusal representation, as the lexical-mediation account suggests. The strongest Llama numbers sit where OOD is high. Random-direction controls (9 directions) support specificity. Qwen3 needs α up to 3.0. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The cited task-specific refusal direction is steered, but the study does not report ablating it at every layer and position or test whether its removal preserves general capabilities. VA steering uses different, emotion-derived directions.
No weight edit or abliteration is tested.
No attack is tested as suppressing the direction, and no training against its ablation is reported.
The study reports a VA subspace and a distinct task-specific direction, but does not compare affine, cone, or dominant-direction-plus-others models as such.
No separate representation of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is tested.
The VA axes are fitted independently for each model; transfer of a fixed direction across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct models is not tested.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or training stages is reported.

relationships.condition: Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct, cited Arditi direction, signed addition
relationships.reason: Negative steering cuts HarmBench refusal from 86.5% to 2.0% (r1). Positive steering raises refusal on safe queries: OKTest 19.7%→93.3% and XSTest 8.4%→94.4% (r2, r3).
relationships.display_finding: Negative steering reduced HarmBench refusal from 86.5% to 2.0%, while positive steering increased safe-query refusal from 19.7% to 93.3% on OKTest and from 8.4% to 94.4% on XSTest.
